Organised whaling at Taiji, a fishing village on the Kii Peninsula in Japan, which became the best known whaling town in the country. A local leader formed a whaling group there in 1606, and later in the 1600s Taiji whalers took up the method of driving whales into nets before harpooning them.

The hunt was a village effort. Lookouts on the cliffs spotted whales, fleets of rowing boats chased them, and hundreds of people cut up and processed the catch. Nothing was wasted: meat, oil for lamps and for killing rice pests, bone and baleen. The method spread along the coasts of western Japan during the Tokugawa period.

In 1878 a disaster at sea killed many Taiji whalers, and coastal whaling declined as modern industrial whaling from steam ships took over. Taiji still hunts dolphins and small whales, drawing world protest after the 2009 film The Cove. Japan defends it as local tradition and in 2019 left the International Whaling Commission to resume commercial whaling.
